# Microsoft press release — cradle-to-grave LCA of datacenter cooling (May 1, 2025)

By Catherine Bolgar, Microsoft Source blog. Companion press release to the Nature paper [17].

## Key figures
- First cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment (LCA) quantifying energy, water and GHG emissions of four datacenter cooling techniques (air cooling, cold plates, one-phase immersion, two-phase immersion) across the entire datacenter lifespan.
- Switching from air cooling to cold plates could reduce GHG emissions and energy demand by roughly 15 percent and water consumption by 30 to 50 percent across the datacenters' entire life spans (including water used in power generation and component manufacturing).
- Cold plates and the two immersion cooling technologies reduce GHG emissions 15 to 21 percent, energy demand 15 to 20 percent, and water consumption 31 to 52 percent vs. air cooling over full life cycles.
- Switching from a typical energy grid to 100 percent renewable energy reduces GHG emissions by 85 to 90 percent regardless of cooling technology.
- Analysis took more than two years; methodology released via open research repository (zenodo.org/records/14268168).
- Paper covers CPUs (general compute), not AI chips; follow-up on AI chips expected.
- Two-phase immersion uses PFAS, under regulatory scrutiny in the EU and US.
- Husam Alissa, director of systems technology in Cloud Operations and Innovation at Microsoft, led the study.

## Quotes
- "A lot of people do life cycle assessments after the fact... We're advocating in this paper for the use of life cycle assessment tools to guide engineering decisions early on." — Husam Alissa
- "What we're trying to do here is tell the industry, 'Here is how you build an end-to-end life cycle assessment that takes cooling into account.'" — Alissa
- "It was interesting to see that cold plates could be as good as the two immersion cooling methods." — Teresa Nick, director, natural systems and sustainability
